US stocks gain as investors parse Anthropic IPO filing
article:
(Oct 26): US stocks gained on Monday as investors digest Anthropic PBC’s filing for its initial public offering (IPO) and look forward to key big tech earnings this week as well as the Federal Reserve’s next decision on Wednesday.

The S&P 500 Index gained 0.9% as of 11.31am in New York, while the Nasdaq 100 was up 1.4%. Brent crude fell 0.42% to US$116 a barrel.

“With so many firms reporting this week, we would typically say that macro factors will take a back seat to idiosyncratic results. However, we have the Fed on Wednesday and what could be a very tricky, complicated press conference,” wrote Christopher Harvey, head of equity and portfolio strategy at CIBC, in a note. “We think Wednesday afternoon will be all about the macro, but by roughly 4.30pm that day, GOOGL and MSFT will take centre stage, and earnings are expected to trump the Fed.”

Anthropic filed its much-awaited S-1, moving a step closer to being the first company focused primarily on developing the most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models to go public. Investors are parsing through all of the facts and figures, with an emphasis on what they mean for AI demand after weeks of doubt in the market.

In addition, Meta Platforms Inc said it is aiming to raise as much as US$95 billion from the sale of common and preferred stock to fund AI spending, and SpaceX signed a roughly US$40 billion equipment-finance lease with Apollo Global Management Inc to pay for the chips needed to fuel its AI ambitions.

See also: CoreWeave rout sends warning sign to rest of stock market

Focus on Monday will also be on the impact from President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s win in Brazil’s runoff election against market favourite Flávio Bolsonaro. US-listed shares of Brazilian companies and those exposed to the country slumped, while the iShares MSCI Brazil ETF tumbled 21%.

Last week was a roller coaster ride for the stock market, with the Nasdaq falling 2.9% on Thursday, a day after Meta raised its capex guidance to above its operating cash flow, spooking investors looking for evidence that massive spending on AI is paying off. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, or SOX, tumbled 6.7% on Thursday, while investors rotated into defensive sectors.

Concerns are spilling into credit, with the price of five-year credit default swaps on Meta’s debt recently spiking to a record high. And on Sunday, Elon Musk wrote in a post on X that “debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centres.”

See also: Growth, value stocks set for reshuffle as S&P adopts new rules

This week will bring more tech results to review, with Alphabet Inc and Microsoft Corp set to report on Wednesday, and Amazon.com Inc and Intel Corp reporting on Thursday. Amid the big tech earnings, investors are also awaiting the Federal Reserve’s meeting on Wednesday, where policymakers are anticipated to leave rates unchanged after raising them in September.

The jitters throughout the market have been enough to turn Max Kettner, chief multi-asset strategist at HSBC, cautious on stocks. The long-time equity bull tactically cut his maximum overweight in stocks to neutral on AI regulation fears heading into the Midterm elections.

In single stock moves, Tesla rose 6.2% as Barclays joins peers on upgrading the electric-car maker, citing M&A opportunity with SpaceX.
• Brazil-linked US stocks are sinking after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise victory.
• Watch bank stocks, as Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Morgan Stanley were listed as leading Anthropic’s IPO, along with several other banks.

title: CoreWeave rout sends warning sign to rest of stock market
article:
(Oct 26): Wall Street strategists are warning that declines in shares of artificial intelligence (AI) cloud-computing providers will spill into other corners of the tech trade, potentially dragging the US stock market down to its June lows.

CoreWeave Inc, the company at the centre of the tumult after its bonds plunged to distressed levels this month, saw its shares drop 41% since Oct 6 as of Friday’s close, when major US equity indices hit a fresh record. Shares of other neoclouds — companies that provide computing power to firms building and running AI models — have also posted double-digit declines during that time. Iren Ltd is down 40% while Nebius Group NV has dropped 36%.

Investors are concerned about the amount of debt companies involved in the AI build-out have borrowed and are worried about how much more they’ll take on after reporting earnings. These fears pushed measures of credit risk for some of the biggest technology companies spending on AI developments to new highs last week.

After a bruising Thursday during which the Nasdaq 100 declined nearly 3% and the S&P 500 had its worst day since late July, strategists see the impact on the equity market deepening.

“It’s now transitioning from being a micro event to a macro event,” Brian Reynolds, chief market strategist at Reynolds Strategy LLC, said of the selloff in neoclouds. “In other words, it’s not just impacting the neoclouds, but the entire credit market and then the stock market.”

Reynolds expects additional selling that could push the S&P 500 back down to its lows of early June. That would mean a 4.7% drop from where the benchmark closed on Friday.

See also: US stocks gain as investors parse Anthropic IPO filing

Neoclouds are massively reliant on issuing bonds to fund their spending. But with US Treasury yields climbing and inflation remaining entrenched, the cost of financing is rising. Ohsung Kwon, chief equity strategist at Wells Fargo & Co, said that if neoclouds cut future capital expenditure plans to assuage investor concerns, that would be a major headwind to semiconductors, whose revenue comes directly from data-centre developers paying huge sums of money for chips.

“If they start to see risk around their financing and the market pushes back on their capex a lot more than what we’re seeing today, and if they cut capex next year, that’s going to be a risk to semis,” Kwon said in an interview.

See also: Growth, value stocks set for reshuffle as S&P adopts new rules

Those fears could come to reality, with Elon Musk warning that the “debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn’t have substantial revenue independent of AI data centres.”

“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote in a post on X on Sunday, referring to guppy fish, which can go in to shock during a change in environment. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

Concerns over neocloud woes have weighed on the Philadelphia Stock Exchange Semiconductor Index, which has dropped more than 13% so far in October.

More than just tech, multiple Wall Street strategists have now warned the meltdown in neoclouds is offering the broader market a reality check at a time when investors are anxious about an AI bubble.

“If the AI bubble is going to burst, it’ll likely start as a credit event as neocloud and risky AI debt defaults, creating a cascade of devaluations, reduced spending and contraction [in multiples and growth],” Sevens Report founder Tom Essaye wrote in a note last week. He added that he’s continuing to watch for signs of stress in the credit markets.

Neocloud stocks are currently showing “asymmetric” responses to credit stresses, according to Barclays plc strategists led by Venu Krishna.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

“Widening spreads prompt outsized declines, while tightening provides limited relief, underscoring skepticism around the neocloud business model’s durability,” they wrote in a note last week.

While Krishna said he was looking for “signs of contagion” in the equity market, he’s not seeing evidence the issue has spread beyond tech and growth stocks just yet. Investors have been rotating out of high-flying technology stocks and into defensive sectors, signalling uncertainty around the AI trade rather than indiscriminate selling when everything gets hit simultaneously.

Still, selling in the market’s largest sector by weight has dragged indices lower. On Thursday, for example, the S&P 500 fell more than 1% even though it had more gainers than decliners.

Reynolds said the US benchmark, which broke below its 50-day moving average on Thursday, may fall all the way to its June lows, at which point he would be a buyer.

“I want to be defensive in the very near term, for a few weeks,” Reynolds said. “I really want to buy at that low 7,200 area.”

title: Apple debuts US$699 water-resistant iPad mini with OLED screen
article:
(Oct 26): Apple Inc on Monday unveiled a revamped iPad mini with an OLED display, water-resistant design and faster chip, kicking off a week of product launches.

The tablet, priced at US$699, features an 8.5-inch OLED, or organic light-emitting diode, screen that delivers deeper blacks, brighter whites and improved contrast. Apple has increased the display size from the previous 8.3 inches by slimming down the bezels around the panel. The redesigned device also includes a new “Acoustic Display” audio system that places the speakers beneath the display, helping to make this the first iPad with an IP67 dust and water resistance rating.

The new iPad mini is 14% thinner and 13% lighter than its predecessor, and Apple has repositioned the front-facing camera so that it’s better suited for FaceTime calls and video conferencing.

Inside, it features the A20 Pro chip, an upgrade from the A17 Pro processor in the previous iPad mini, which started at US$599. It’s being offered with standard and matte nano-texture display options and storage configurations ranging from 128 gigabytes (GB) to 512GB. Fully outfitted with the maximum amount of storage, an etched matte screen and cellular connectivity, the tablet can cost as much as US$1,249.

Apple has also upgraded the new model with its N1 networking chip, bringing WiFi 7 and Bluetooth 6 to the iPad mini. Cellular models are equipped with the company’s C2 modem.

The latest iPad mini kicks off a series of late-October product introductions from Apple. Later this week, the company plans to unveil a new iMac and 14-inch MacBook Pro with the M6 chip, before closing out the week with its first touch-screen MacBook Pro.

See also: Apple's iPhone Duo hits stores in face of short supply, high demand

Pre-orders for the new iPad mini begin on Wednesday and it goes on sale on Nov 6. The latest model comes in “midnight” and “starlight” colour options.

The A20 Pro chip on the iPad mini is being offered in two versions: The 128GB and 256GB models include five CPU, or main processing cores, while the higher-end configuration has six cores. Both use seven graphics cores. The higher-end variant also has a dual 16-core Neural Engine for enhanced artificial intelligence processing.

Apple is holding a launch event on Wednesday in Los Angeles, where members of the press and content creators will get hands-on time with the new devices. The introductions cap a busy year of product releases for Apple, including last Friday’s launch of the iPhone Duo, its first foldable smartphone.

See also: UK said to push for carve-out from new EU tech sovereignty rules

Bloomberg News first reported on the new iPad mini last year. The company is also working on a new low-end iPad, OLED iPad Air and refreshed iPad Pro for the first half of next year.

title: Anthropic flags ‘existential risks’ in long-awaited IPO filing
article:
(Oct 26): Anthropic PBC filed for an initial public offering (IPO), warning its technology carried existential risks even as it moved a step closer to being the first company focused primarily on developing the most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models to go public.

The company behind Claude expects to begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT, a filing on Monday with the US Securities and Exchange Commission showed. Anthropic filed confidentially in June for a listing.

The IPO is being led Goldman Sachs Group Inc and Morgan Stanley, along with 20 other banks, the filing showed. Anthropic and some of its shareholders are offering stock in the IPO, according to the filing. The amount of shares they are offering will be disclosed in a later filing.

The company’s debut has become a focal point for the world’s hopes and fears over AI, which run the gamut from worries over job displacement and the substantial upfront spending the technology needs to other, more existential questions: Anthropic’s prospectus has flagged various “risks to humanity” including attempts to “resist shutdown” and “conceal or manipulate information”.

Anthropic had an US$80.7 billion ($103.4 billion) net loss on revenue of US$16.3 billion in the first six months of 2026, versus a US$13 billion net loss on revenue of US$1.2 billion in the same period last year, the filing showed.

The company has mainly focused on serving the enterprise market. Anthropic’s net revenue retention, a measure of its ability to keep its existing customers and increase their spending over time, is about 900%, the filing showed.

See also: Sembcorp gauges demand for US$394 mil India unit IPO — Bloomberg

Anthropic said 79% of its revenue came from customers outside of its top five customers for the third quarter of the year.

Anthropic is seeking to tap the public market’s ample funding capacity to maintain its lead over rivals, as AI companies burn through hundreds of billions of dollars to continue advancing their so-called frontier models.

See also: Mi Material to be spun off from Bursa-listed parent; bets on China+1 for growth

It is set to begin formally marketing for its IPO as soon as the week of Nov 9, Bloomberg News has reported. Anthropic expects to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s record-setting IPO, people familiar with the matter have said.

The company and its rival OpenAI are also facing mounting public scrutiny over AI safety after a string of high-profile hacking incidents by rogue agents, ramping up concern about the potential impact on Anthropic’s market debut.

Anthropic emphasised the potential for its AI to “behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways” in the filing. If its technologies are not developed with adequate safeguards and oversight, it could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy”.

Consumption-based revenue rose from US$288 million, and 75% of the company’s revenue, for the year that ended Dec 31, 2024 to US$3.8 billion, and 83% of the total, for last year. Information technology made up US$13.1 billion, and 80% of revenue, between January and June of this year. For Anthropic, consumption-based revenue refers to customers that pay for its AI models as they use them, based on the amount of tokens and the type of AI model they use.

The company’s total indebtedness stood at US$6.2 billion as of June 30, and it said it could raise more debt going forward to meet its financing needs.

Anthropic said it has a revolving credit facility of up US$15 billion, which it increased in size from US$3.25 billion. Revolving loans work much like a credit card, allowing a company to borrow, repay and borrow again up to a set limit over the life of the facility. They are commonly used by companies to provide financial flexibility and ready access to liquidity when needed. The revolver will mature in 2031, the company said.

It added that, after obtaining an investment-grade credit rating from at least two of the three major credit rating agencies, the revolving loan could become unsecured.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

The company spent US$8.9 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the six months that ended June 30, up 283% from the year prior. The company noted that these expenses declined as a percentage of revenue, seemingly responding to concerns about the pace of spending.

Just since the end of 2025, Anthropic entered into new agreements for computing power with minimum obligations of about US$417 billion. These agreements will generally start this year or next, with terms as long as 20 years.

Anthropic’s compute economics have improved as revenue has scaled. Compute and infrastructure spending was more than 10 times revenue in 2023, falling to 653% in 2024, 160% in 2025 and just 55% in the first half of 2026. In the second quarter alone, it fell further to 48% of revenue — meaning Anthropic was spending about 48 cents on compute and infrastructure for every dollar of sales.

Goldman Sachs touted its role in the coveted lead-left position in marketing documents sent to clients, after securing the same role for the record-setting listing of SpaceX earlier this year, a document seen by Bloomberg showed. Morgan Stanley, its rival, is the so-called stabilisation agent, a sought-after role that would see it engage in transactions that reduce volatility in the stock, the filing showed.

title: SpaceX agrees to US$40 bil chip-financing deal with Apollo
article:
(Oct 26): SpaceX signed a roughly US$40 billion ($51.25 billion) equipment-finance lease with Apollo Global Management Inc to pay for the chips needed to fuel its artificial intelligence (AI) ambitions.

The fixed-rate that the company will pay will be determined at pricing, which hasn’t yet occurred, SpaceX said in a filing on Monday. The deal is expected to close before year end, and the leases are expected to start in the first half of next year.

Elon Musk touted the deal to help finance purchases of Nvidia Corp’s graphics processing units in a post on X over the weekend.

“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX said in a statement on Monday, adding that it’s seeing “less than one year payback periods” on its AI investments.

The agreement comes on the heels of a tumultuous week for AI companies in debt markets as concern mounted over the industry’s rapid spending, and limited profits so far to show for it. With investors demanding increasingly large premiums to finance the AI build-out, the volatility roiled pricing discussions over the SpaceX debt, which is being structured as private bonds to be issued by an off-balance sheet entity.

Much of the investor angst has been focused on the so-called neoclouds, which sell high-end computing power to technology companies. Musk has sought to differentiate his company from those businesses, pointing to SpaceX’s revenue from its Starlink business and rocket launches.

See also: Dutch government plans to cut 25,000 jobs in AI-led overhaul

SpaceX, which is rated investment-grade by the three largest credit graders, has seen the price of its own debt tumble in recent weeks. Credit-default swaps tied to the company, which are used to insure against losses on its debt, surged last week to a record 266 basis points at the close of trading last Friday, a level more typical of a junk-rated borrower. That concern eased slightly in early trading on Monday, with SpaceX swaps trading around 261 basis points, ICE Data Services prices showed.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc served as the sole structuring agent on the deal, according to the statement. Funds and accounts managed by BlackRock Inc, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and capital accounts advised by KKR & Co also made anchor commitments.

title: PM Burnham says he wants UK to rejoin EU in his lifetime
article:
(Oct 26): Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wants the UK to rejoin the European Union (EU) during his lifetime, calling for an “honest” discussion about the impact of Brexit.

“I don’t think things have worked out as people said they would,” Burnham told ITV of his country’s 2016 decision to leave the bloc, adding that he wasn’t proposing any changes during this Parliament. “I’m going to lead a discussion on how we make it better.”

Reshaping Britain’s relationship with the European Union has become one of Burnham’s key pledges since he became the prime minister three months ago, as he gambles on revisiting a divisive issue that dominated UK politics over the last decade. The 56-year-old prime minister opened the door to rejoining the EU at his party’s annual conference last month, saying he would set out options for a new relationship later this year.

Burnham said he wouldn’t seek to re-run the 2016 referendum, nor break Labour’s 2024 election pledge not to join the EU’s single market or customs union.

He was speaking ahead of a UK-EU summit which is due to take place on Nov 20, when the prime minister has said he wants to make progress on boosting economic growth and tackling illegal immigration into the UK.

See also: Axel Springer to cut Telegraph jobs after buying UK newspaper

Burnham said he’s seeking a deal that aims “to support our farmers, our food manufacturers, but also to increase collaboration on immigration because we lost that and we need to get it back”, he told Sky News later on Monday. “I’m talking about practical steps to deal with the things that matter to people.”

He said the UK had stronger return agreements for the arrival of people in small boats when it was in the EU, and that immigrants have now become more likely to settle in the country permanently, rather than leaving after a few years.

He added that he will “never move ahead” of public opinion on the issue of Brexit, though it’s unclear how he intends to achieve that. Asked whether Burnham would use a referendum or a general election to gain a mandate for his new EU position, his deputy official spokeswoman Cat Simmons declined to comment.

See also: UK set to ease up on senior bankers in bid to save firms £2 bil

“We’re not at that stage yet,” Simmons said to reporters at a briefing on Monday. “The first step here is the substance rather than the process.”

Burnham also used the ITV interview to rule out an early election, saying it’s not something he’s thinking about.

“There is no election coming any time soon,” he said. “Britain is starting to regain its momentum.”

title: Soybeans hit two-month low as Lula’s win lifts China trade outlook
article:
(Oct 26): Soybean futures fell to a two-month low in Chicago, while coffee and sugar slumped as President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s surprise election win in Brazil hit the nation’s currency, boosting export prospects for the commodity powerhouse.

 

Lula won a fourth term, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro in a political upset that comes as a setback to investors who had backed his rival to rein in the country’s deficit. Brazilian markets are heading for a rout when local trading begins with a currency derivatives contract on the CME exchange showing the real at 5.60 a dollar, which implies a 12% plunge from Friday’s close. Trading on the real opens at 8am New York time.

A weaker real boosts the competitiveness of Brazilian produce, encouraging exports as farmers receive more local currency for their crops. As Brazil is the world’s biggest exporter of sugar, coffee and soy, that’s bearish for prices.

 

The most-actively traded soybean contract on the Chicago Board of Trade dropped as much as 1.7% to the lowest since late August. Lula’s emphasis on pragmatic engagement with China could further entrench Brazil’s dominance as the Asian nation’s top soybean supplier and erode the US’s share of the world’s biggest soybean import market.

Brazil has increasingly taken more market share in China, accounting for nearly 80% of its imports in the first nine months of the year, despite Beijing’s trade deal with the US, its No 2 supplier. At the same time, China has boosted investment in the South American country’s port infrastructure, including terminals at Santos built by top crop trader Cofco Corp.

“Lula is pro exports of beans to China, so that is bearish US soybeans if Brazil can fulfill more of China’s needs,” said Joe Davis, director of commodity sales at Futures International LLC.

The weakness spilled over into edible oils, with soyoil futures dropping as much as 1.2% in Chicago and palm oil falling as much as 1.1% in Kuala Lumpur, snapping a two-day advance. Palm oil typically tracks soyoil because they compete for many of the same food and biofuel markets.

See also: Copper slumps as surging stocks and tech-stock selloff sour mood

Elevated Malaysian inventories also weighed on the market despite an improvement in export demand, according to Tasvinderjit Singh, director and head of futures at CGS International Futures Malaysia.

Sugar and coffee futures also dropped when trading opened on Monday. The most-actively traded sugar contract fell as much as 3.6%, the most in over a month, while arabica coffee dropped as much as 3.3%. Robusta fell to a two-year low.

The move is a “simple technical reaction” to the expected currency move, according to Arnaud Lorioz, chief executive officer of Paris-based brokerage Deepcore. “The market is saying the real will favour more exports from sugar producers in Brazil.”

See also: Nickel rallies past US$16,000 on prospect of Indonesia output cuts

Lula’s re-election brings his nation’s relationship with the US into question, given his ideological differences with President Donald Trump. In July, the US president hit Brazil with a 25% tariff, but Trump has also praised Lula’s intelligence and found him to be a “good man”.

The way the relationship between the two leaders develops could have longer-term impacts on agricultural markets, said Carlos Mera, head of agricultural commodities research at Rabobank. “The US can impose a number of measures on countries that they see as enemies,” he added.
• Soybeans dropped 1.4% to US$12.53 a bushel as of 10.20am in London
• Raw sugar was 2.3% lower in New York
